codes.sample: Ethnobotanical tea bar patrons at two bars in northern Colorado, USA, recruited by street intercept. 102 surveyed; 4 who had never used kratom were excluded, leaving N=98 for survey 1. A subset of N=50 rated the subjective effects of kratom in survey 2. Mean age 22.34; 54.6% men. Data were collected before July 1, 2024.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime any use: the 4 people who had never used kratom were excluded. Current frequency was recorded (73.4% weekly, 19.3% daily), and 9.2% said they had tried kratom but no longer use it.
codes.dependence_measures: None for kratom. Only general SUD items: clinician-diagnosed SUD (11.3%) and believing one met SUD criteria (51.6%), neither specific to kratom. Other measures: DEQ, ARCI, BAES. Withdrawal (N=3) and addiction (N=1) appear only as qualitative themes.
codes.note: Kratom use disorder or dependence was not assessed with any instrument. The SUD items in Table 2 (p.26) are general, not about kratom, and withdrawal and addiction come only from open-text answers (Table 5, p.29). The discussion confirms this: 'More research is needed to determine whether bar patrons are at increased or decreased risk for development of KUD' (p.16).

codes.sample: 20 consecutive adult chronic pain patients with documented comorbid substance misuse receiving monthly IM ketamine (0.25 mg/kg) at a specialist pain clinic in Canada, Jan 2022–Dec 2023. Primary misuse category kratom in 2/20 (10%), both male.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Kratom as the primary 'substance misuse category' (clinic-documented); no reference period or definition of use given.
codes.dependence_measures: Severity of Dependence Scale (SDS), range 0-15, '≤ 6 considered satisfactory and ≥ 7 unsatisfactory'. Results are reported only as a qualitative whole-cohort statement; there is no SDS figure for the kratom users.
codes.possible_duplicate: Registered as NCT05985811 (Salem Anaesthesia Pain Clinic, Surrey, BC). Other reports from this group may use the same clinic cohort.
codes.note: Calls itself 'a descriptive case series' (p.2) of 20 patients, so the primary reason is E5. Other reasons would also apply. The sample was selected for substance misuse (arguably E1 for the kratom cases). SDS is reported only for the whole cohort ('improved from the unsatisfactory range (≥7) to 5', p.5), with no count for the 2 kratom users (E2/no_extractable_counts).

codes.sample: Czech university students. Anonymous online Google Forms survey shared through student and kratom-user Facebook groups, 28 Feb to 20 Mar 2025. N=287 respondents. 85 reported ever using kratom: 40 regular users, 20 occasional users, 25 who had used it once or twice. Questions 6 to 15 were answered by these 85 users only.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime any use: "Užíváte nebo jste někdy užívali kratom?" ("Do you use or have you ever used kratom?"). Among the 85 users, 33 (38.8%) used daily.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The 20-item self-made questionnaire covered use frequency, form of use, motives, positive and adverse effects, perceived risks and legislation. It used no DSM, ICD, SDS, KDS or ASSIST measure. Dependence appears only as a perceived risk (90.6%) and in free-text comments.
codes.note: Czech bachelor thesis. "Riziko vzniku závislosti" (risk of developing dependence) is a perceived-risk item, not a measure. Two people mentioned severe dependence in free text only. The abstract says 87 participants, while the methods say 287 ("Dotazník vyplnilo celkem 287 respondentů"); 287 matches the counts. Withdrawal appears only in free-text adverse effects.

codes.sample: Not reported. The text received is only the assignment sheet. It describes a planned questionnaire survey ("dotaz.šetření zaměřené na vybranou populaci") of children and adolescents in the Czech Republic. No sample size, recruitment details or results are given.

codes.dependence_measures: Not reported. The sheet mentions only "Možnosti depistáže a diagnostiky" (options for screening and diagnosis). No instrument or cut-off is named.

(kratom)... kvantitativního výzkumu" (specify kratom risk using quantitative research). Get the full thesis PDF from the VŠB-TUO repository and check it against I1–I4.

codes.sample: Pilot case-control SPECT-CT imaging study, Universiti Sains Malaysia (Penang/Kelantan, Malaysia): 12 male "kratom-dependent subjects" (aged 31.58 ± 11.28) who volunteered, plus 13 healthy male controls. Kratom intake 2.13 ± 1.68 L/day (range 0.5-6), use duration 9.92 ± 6.54 years. All kratom users smoked.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Current regular (daily) kratom drinking. Participants were recruited because they were kratom-dependent; quantity is given in L/day. The text gives no further reference period.
codes.dependence_measures: "Kratom addiction was assessed using the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-V)". Only a mean score is reported ("severe addiction to kratom, with a total mean score of nine", Figure 1). HAM-A was used for withdrawal symptoms.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same USM group may have other imaging or neuropsychological papers using this sample of kratom-dependent men (USM/JEPeM/20020113, FRGS/1/2019/SKK08/USM/03/4). Check for overlap.
codes.note: Being kratom-dependent was the entry criterion, so any proportion would be 100% by design. These are not treatment cases, so the reviewer may prefer 'other'. DSM-5 results are only a mean score of 9 (Figure 1) with no counts by severity category, so no_extractable_counts would also apply.

codes.sample: 100 adult men who use kratom daily, recruited by purposive and convenience sampling in the community in Penang, Malaysia (Nov 2024–Jan 2025). Inclusion: aged 18+, self-reported regular user, used kratom at least once daily in the past year. 99 Malay, 1 Chinese, mean age 44.07. Recruited for regular use, not from kratom treatment.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Self-reported regular kratom use, at least once daily in the last one year (i.e. daily use in the past 12 months). Mainly kratom juice/boiled leaf decoction.
codes.dependence_measures: Kratom Dependence Scale (KDS; Saingam et al. 2014), 16 items scored 0–3, past-12-month reference. Severity bands as reported: 0-13 = mild; 14-34 = moderate; 35-48 = severe. There is no 'no dependence' band, so every respondent falls in at least 'mild'.

codes.sample: Clients of 10 Cure and Care Service Centres (CCSC) in Peninsular Malaysia who used services in 2011-2012 (at least 6 months before the interview). Table 1 lists 323 sampled clients, and 232 are reported as respondents. Of these, 100 (31.3%) said they consumed ketum leaves before CCSC and 17 (5.7%) after.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Table 3 item "Consume Ketum Leaves (Mitragynine sp)", reported before CCSC (100, 31.3%) and after CCSC (17, 5.7%). The reference period is not stated (it covers the time before and after the programme).
codes.dependence_measures: ASSIST is described only as the CCSC's routine intake tool for assigning low/moderate/high severity (0-3, 4-26, high). No ASSIST or other dependence or use-disorder results are reported for kratom. The study's outcome interview measured only whether each substance was used.
codes.note: Outcome evaluation of a community drug treatment programme. Ketum use appears only as yes/no counts before and after ("drinking ketum has reduced from 100 to 17", p.4). ASSIST is named on p.2 as the programme's intake tool, but no ASSIST bands or other dependence figures are given for kratom users. Denominators are inconsistent (323 sampled vs 232 respondents).

codes.sample: 357 U.S. adults who regularly use kratom and completed all 15 days of an EMA study (395 enrolled at baseline). Recruited online July–November 2022 through social media, kratom advocacy groups, vendors and podcasts. Mean age 38.0; 55.5% male; 91.0% non-Hispanic White; 37.8% in recovery from alcohol or other drugs; 49% had chronic pain.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Regular use: "at least three times per week for a minimum of four weeks before screening".
codes.dependence_measures: None reported. Measures were bedtime kratom use, sleep duration, sleep quality (VAS item adapted from the Consensus Sleep Diary), sex, and chronic pain (Brief Pain Inventory item). No DSM-5, ICD, SDS, KDS, ASSIST or other kratom dependence measure is described.
codes.possible_duplicate: Secondary analysis of the NIH 15-day EMA study of U.S. kratom consumers (n=395 at baseline, Jul–Nov 2022). Parent papers: Smith, Panlilio, Feldman et al. 2024; Smith, Feldman et al. 2024; Mun et al. 2025. Check the parents for kratom use disorder data.
codes.note: This secondary EMA analysis is about bedtime kratom use and sleep. No kratom use disorder or dependence measure or estimate appears in the text. Table 1 (participant characteristics) is not reproduced in the text received, but the narrative description of Table 1 mentions no dependence measure. Supplementary Tables 1–2 hold only sensitivity-model estimates.

codes.sample: 357 US adults who use kratom, recruited nationally for a 15-day smartphone EMA study, July–October/November 2022. 56.6% male, 90.2% non-Hispanic white. 348 completed EMA and submitted product samples for alkaloid assay.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Regular current use: 'they reported using kratom >3 times/week for > 4 weeks, among other criteria'.
codes.dependence_measures: None reported in this text. Outcomes are EMA-rated felt effects (0–100), product form, amount used and assayed alkaloid content. No DSM-5, ICD, dependence scale or ASSIST results are given.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same national EMA sample (n=357, 2022, NIH IRB) as Smith et al. 2023a (methods) and Smith et al. 2024a (initial results and baseline survey). The text says Table 1 covers demographics and the strain usually used, but the table itself is not in the retrieved text. The reviewer should check that Table 1 has no DSM-5 data, and should screen Smith et al. 2024a, which uses the same sample.

codes.sample: Retrospective medical record review of 9,606 new psychiatric-clinic patients aged 18+ (some <18 in the tables) with a primary SUD diagnosis by a psychiatrist, at 16 Malaysian government tertiary hospitals, 2018–2021. Kratom listed among substances used: 841 (8.8%) in total, by year 185/217/273/166.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Kratom recorded as a 'type of substance abuse' in the medical record (self-report, doctor notes, urine drug test). No reference period given.
codes.dependence_measures: Whole-sample SUD diagnosis by the psychiatrist in charge. The SUD is not tied to a substance, and no DSM/ICD criteria, scale or cut-off were applied to kratom specifically.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Malaysian multicentre hospital record study (16 hospitals, 2018–2021, N=9,606; NMRR-21-1275-60439).
codes.note: All patients had some SUD, but its substance is not stated. Kratom is only one of the substances used (Table 2: 'Kratom | 841 (8.8)'), with no kratom-specific use-disorder count. 56.8% used several substances. E2 is a possible alternative reason. Supporting information files were not in the text received; worth checking for diagnoses by substance.

codes.sample: 102 patrons recruited by street intercept at two ethnobotanical tea bars in northern Colorado, USA, aged 18 or older, surveyed before July 2024. After excluding 4 who had never used kratom, N=98 lifetime kratom users completed survey 1 (mean age 22.34; 39.2% women). N=50 reported on acute subjective effects in survey 2.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime any use: participants who reported never using kratom were excluded (p.7). This includes 9 people (9.2%) who had tried kratom but no longer used it. Weekly use was reported by 73.4% and daily use by 19.3%.
codes.dependence_measures: No kratom use-disorder or dependence measure. The survey asked about any SUD diagnosed by a clinician and any self-perceived SUD, not specific to kratom. Open-text adverse reactions included withdrawal (N=3) and 'addiction to kratom' (N=1). Other measures were DEQ, ARCI and BAES subjective effects.
codes.possible_duplicate: None apparent. This appears to be a single study at two northern Colorado tea bars (N=98 kratom users).
codes.note: Diagnosed SUD (11.3%) and perceived SUD (51.6%) refer to substance use disorder in general, not kratom. The discussion (p.15–16) notes that KUD was not assessed and calls for more research. The 'Addiction to kratom (N=1)' code comes from qualitative open-text answers, not a case definition.

codes.sample: Anonymous international online survey of current kratom users (Qualtrics, July 2019–July 2020; recruited via Facebook/Reddit groups and the American Kratom Association website). This sub-study: n=70 who completed the COVID-19 section added in January 2020, out of 4,945 completed surveys. Also 379 social media posts from March–July 2020.
codes.kratom_use_definition: "Current kratom users", identified by "How long has it been since you first consumed Kratom?". No clear reference period; 7.8% reported only "sporadic use in the past".
codes.dependence_measures: None. The survey asked about demographics, reasons for use, sources, dose, frequency, dose increase over time, co-use with other drugs, pain/health VAS and COVID-19 questions. Dependence appears only as a qualitative social media theme.
codes.possible_duplicate: Sub-study of a larger international online kratom survey (University of Florida IRB #2019–01121, July 2019–July 2020, 4,945 completed surveys); parent data described as "forthcoming". Other papers from it may include a dependence measure.
codes.note: No DSM, ICD, scale or ASSIST measure for kratom. The only related item is "Did you increase the regular dose of Kratom over the course of time?" (Yes 31, 40.3%), which is not a case definition. The supplement (survey instrument, Tables S1/S2) was not received, but the Methods say only demographic and COVID questions were analysed.

codes.sample: Community cross-sectional survey of 238 ethnically diverse adolescents aged 15-17 (Tai Yai, Yunnanese Chinese, Akha, Lahu, Hmong), Therd Thai subdistrict, Mae Fah Luang district, Chiang Rai, Thailand. Simple random sampling, data collected Dec 2024-Feb 2025 by online questionnaire. Kratom users: 44/238 (18.5%).
codes.kratom_use_definition: "การใช้พืชกระท่อม ใช้ 44 (18.5%)" (Table 1), i.e. kratom use, assessed with the Thai ASSIST. The reference period is not stated (could be lifetime or past 3 months).
codes.dependence_measures: Thai ASSIST (V3.1, ref. 21) covering tobacco, alcohol, cannabis and kratom. Bands for substances other than alcohol: low risk 0-3, moderate 4-26, high ≥27. No ASSIST risk-band results are reported for kratom or for any other substance.
codes.possible_duplicate: No overlap found. Sample: Therd Thai subdistrict, Chiang Rai, Dec 2024-Feb 2025, n=238 adolescents (Mae Fah Luang University).

Results give only use prevalence (44/238, 18.5%) and ORs. No kratom risk-band counts. Authors could be contacted for these. Vol 52(1), 2026 (header misprints 2029).

codes.sample: 26 male active (daily/regular) ketum users from the northern states of Peninsular Malaysia (Penang, Kedah). They were recruited partly through key informants for a human laboratory study (COWS withdrawal after 12 h cessation; cold pressor task, ketum vs placebo) at Pusat Sejahtera, USM. PhD thesis, 2022. They were not recruited because of kratom problems.
codes.kratom_use_definition: "Active" ketum users. The research questions say "daily kratom users" and the hypotheses say "regular kratom users", meaning current regular or daily use. The exact inclusion criteria (section 3.4.1) are not in the text received.
codes.dependence_measures: Ketum Dependence Scale (KDS): methods in 3.6.2, results in 4.2.5 and "Table 4.1 Mean values of ketum dependence scale (KDS) based on the domains of use". Version and any cut-off are not visible in the text received. COWS was also used (withdrawal only).
codes.possible_duplicate: This may share participants with publications from the USM Centre for Drug Research (Vicknasingam, Chawarski, Singh) on the same laboratory/clinical trial of 26 male regular ketum users in Penang/Kedah. Check whether a journal article reports KDS data for this sample.
codes.note: The text stops at section 2.4 (about page 24); methods 3.6.2, results 4.2.5, Table 4.1 and Table 4.6 are missing. The table of contents suggests KDS is reported only as means by domain. If the full text gives no cut-off-based proportion, the likely decision is not_eligible with reason no_extractable_counts. The full results chapter is needed.

codes.sample: Study 1: a remote national US sample of adults who use kratom regularly, recruited July–October 2022. 395 completed the survey, 357 completed EMA, and 309 drivers were analysed in clusters A–E (39/60/65/72/73). Study 2: an in-person substudy of n=10 at NIDA IRP Baltimore.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Regular use, defined as "using kratom regularly (≥3 times weekly for ≥4 consecutive weeks)". Past 30-day kratom use was also recorded.
codes.dependence_measures: None reported. The outcomes were the Driving Habits Questionnaire, pilot items on driving after kratom, EMA VAS ratings of impairment and driving confidence, PSQI, KSS and simulated driving. No DSM-5, SDS, KDS or other dependence instrument applied to kratom is reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is the same national remote survey/EMA cohort as Smith et al. 2023b and Smith et al. 2024 (US, July–Oct 2022, n=395 survey / 357 EMA; NCT05457803). Companion papers from this cohort may report kratom use-disorder outcomes and could be eligible instead.
codes.note: The paper focuses only on driving. The text says "Additional Study 1 outcomes are reported elsewhere (Smith et al., 2024)". Physical dependence is mentioned only speculatively in the Introduction, and no dependence measure is reported. Supplementary material was not in the text received, but it is described as containing product and demographic tables and EMA figures, not dependence data.

codes.sample: UK residents who answered an online NPS survey (Bristol Online Survey). It was advertised on Bluelight, DS Daily, Facebook and University of Hertfordshire email. 2015 wave: n=98 UK respondents, 17 NPS users (7 Jan–7 Feb 2015). 2017 wave: n=500 UK respondents, 134 NPS users (9 Mar–18 Sep 2017). The paper gives no separate n for kratom users.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime NPS use (asked of those who had 'taken an NPS on at least one occasion in the past'). Kratom appears only in the list of 'Other' NPS types in the Figure 2 legend, for both waves. The paper gives no count of kratom users.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The survey covered awareness, use, sources, settings, reasons/motivations, subjective effects and perceived health risk. It used no use-disorder or dependence instrument for kratom or for any other substance.
codes.possible_duplicate: The 2015 wave overlaps with Deligianni et al. 2017, Human Psychopharmacology (international NPS survey, 168 responses). The 2017 data were also presented at the VIth International NPS conference (Research and Advances in Psychiatry 2019). Neither is relevant, because the report is not eligible.
codes.note: Kratom is mentioned only in the Figure 2 legend (p. 28): '2017 Other included kratom, ...' and '2015 Other included kratom, ...'. The paper reports no kratom-specific count and no measure of dependence or use disorder.

codes.sample: 10 healthy male chronic regular kratom users in Thailand (Ramathibodi Hospital, Bangkok). They were recruited for a prospective experimental pharmacokinetic study of kratom tea made in 2012–2013. Mean age was 27.1±4.7 years. Median duration of use was 1.75 years (range 0.6–5), and median use was 4 leaves per day (range 1–9).
codes.kratom_use_definition: Inclusion: "using Kratom regularly for more than 6 months, having positive urine or blood test for mitragynine at the first hospital visit". This is current regular use, confirmed by a lab test.
codes.dependence_measures: None. Participants had only "medical, physical, and basic psychological evaluations". No DSM, ICD, KDS, SDS, ASSIST or diagnostic interview was applied to kratom.
codes.note: Human pharmacokinetic study in kratom users, so E7 does not apply because participants use kratom. A pharmacokinetic experiment is not an E5 category. Reported: demographics, use duration, leaves per day, pharmacokinetic parameters and vital signs only. No use-disorder or dependence measure. The text calls use "abuse" but never assesses it.

codes.sample: US adults on Amazon Mechanical Turk who reported past-6-month alcohol, opioid, kratom and/or stimulant use, Sept–Dec 2020. 1,510 evaluable respondents; 202 (13.4%) reported lifetime kratom use and 123 (8.1%) past-year use.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime kratom use (at least once), n=202; past-year use n=123.
codes.dependence_measures: DSM-5 SUD checklist, completed only for the substance each respondent named as their biggest problem (or used most often) in the past year. Mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe ≥6 criteria. The authors say they did not assess kratom use disorder.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same NIH IRP mTurk survey (Sept–Dec 2020, N=1,510) as later follow-up papers by Smith, Epstein et al. that recontacted the kratom users identified here.
codes.note: The only figure for kratom users covers any substance: 'Most (83.2%) met diagnostic criteria for any past-year SUD.' The text says: 'we did not assess criteria for kratom use disorder.' E2 is a possible alternative reason, because the checklist may have been applied to kratom for some respondents, but no kratom figure is reported.

codes.sample: 644 current kratom users (target population: people who use kratom regularly) surveyed anonymously online via Qualtrics, 22 July–12 Sept 2022. Recruited through newsletters sent to customers of US vendor Super Speciosa. Mostly American, Caucasian and middle-aged; 56.6% male.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Current kratom users ("Six hundred forty-four current kratom users"); "The target population of this survey were people who use kratom regularly." No reference period was stated.

codes.sample: Male long-term kratom users (LKU) who chew fresh leaves, from Ban Nasarn district (Surat Thani) and Natavee district (Songkhla), southern Thailand. 38 LKU recruited, 28 met inclusion criteria (alongside 24 controls). Mean age 52.41 ± 15.45; 85.71% farmers; mean duration of use 26.85 ± 11.11 years; mean 10.39 ± 7.20 leaves/day. Not recruited because of kratom problems.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Current long-term kratom leaf chewing. The appended IEEE article (Fig. 1 note) says LKU had to have used kratom for ≥2 years and to have last used it at least 2 hours before testing. Reference period: current long-term regular use.
codes.dependence_measures: Krathom Dependence Scale (KDS; Saingam et al., 2014), 16 items, described as 'based on' DSM-IV (printed as 'DSM-VI'), self-rated by LKU. Fixed bands as printed: low 0-13, moderate 13-34, high 35-48 (alpha 0.97).
codes.possible_duplicate: Same sample (28 male LKU, 24 controls; Surat Thani/Songkhla; ethics HSc-HREC-63-017-1-1) as Saengmolee et al. 2022, IEEE Sensors J 22(6):6088, appended to the thesis; that article reports no KDS bands. A related HRV paper (19 LKU) was under revision.
codes.note: The KDS bands are fixed score ranges, not derived from the sample, but they overlap at 13 ('0-13' and '13-34'). Check them against the original Saingam 2014 cut-off. The mean is printed as '25.07 ± 96', likely a typo. Path analysis used n=24. Only men were included. The KDS bands are the only case definition; no DSM diagnosis was made.

codes.sample: 26 male Malay adults (mean age 24.3, SD 3.4) recruited in Penang state, Malaysia, May–August 2018, for a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind inpatient study of kratom decoction and cold pressor pain tolerance. All were otherwise healthy daily kratom users (mean 6.1, SD 3.2 years of daily use).
codes.kratom_use_definition: Eligibility: "reported daily kratom intake during the past 12 months". Use in the 7 days before admission was recorded with Timeline Follow Back (TLFB).
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only related measure was the Clinical Opioid Withdrawal Scale (COWS), used as a withdrawal measure during 10–20 h without kratom (mean scores only). The authors state the design "precluded evaluations of addictive potential of kratom."
codes.possible_duplicate: The same 2018 Penang/USM inpatient sample (n=26 males, NCT03414099) is to be used for a separate mitragynine pharmacokinetic paper ("will be reported in a separate publication"). Neither paper is expected to give dependence estimates.
codes.note: This is an experimental RCT in daily kratom users. It used no DSM, ICD, KDS, SDS, ASSIST or other use-disorder or dependence measure for kratom. Withdrawal was assessed with COWS only, reported as mean scores (e.g., baseline 0.5 (0.8)), so the report meets exclusion E4.

codes.sample: US adults aged over 21, recruited online (social media, email listservs, podcasts) through MoreBetter Ltd. They used a commercial liquid full-spectrum kratom extract (20 mg mitragynine per serving) for 2 weeks after a 7-day baseline. The full dataset had 82 participants; 35 completed all 21 days (Section 3.2 gives n = 41). Previous kratom use: 15 (36.6%).
codes.kratom_use_definition: Self-selected, self-reported daily use of the study kratom product during a 2-week observation period. Use was logged in daily evening surveys and grouped post hoc by dose (20 mg; 21–40 mg mitragynine equivalent).
codes.dependence_measures: None. The outcomes were daily 5-point Likert items on focus, productivity, fatigue and energy, 0–10 pain ratings, and self-reported negative effects per session. No DSM, ICD, dependence scale or ASSIST for kratom was used.
codes.possible_duplicate: Described as a secondary analysis of a real-world longitudinal observational dataset from MoreBetter Ltd. (US, n = 82 enrolled, 35 completers). Other analyses of the same dataset may exist.
codes.note: Observational effectiveness study of a kratom product. Dependence is mentioned only in the Discussion, citing other literature (p. 10: "Kratom dependency and withdrawal symptoms are dose and duration dependent..."). No dependence assessment was done. Completer n is inconsistent: Section 2.4 says 35, Section 3.2 says 41, and Tables 3–4 use different denominators.

codes.sample: Cross-sectional community study, Nam Phu sub-district, Surat Thani, Southern Thailand: 285 traditional kratom users (224 male, 61 female; mean age 55.8) and 296 age-matched non-users, all aged ≥18 and resident ≥1 year. Kratom users were people officially registered under the community charter.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Past 12 months: "individuals who had used kratom within the past 12 months and were officially registered under the community charter agreement". Duration of use (years) and daily number of leaves were recorded.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The structured questionnaire covered sociodemographics, health behaviours, medical history, medication, and kratom duration and quantity. Outcomes were hematological and clinical-chemistry parameters. No DSM, ICD, KDS, SDS or ASSIST measure is reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: Nam Phu sub-district surveillance project, Surat Thani (ethics WU-EC-AH-2-144-63; n=581: 285 users, 296 non-users). The same cohort was used for earlier papers on lipids (ref 8) and metabolic syndrome (ref 9). Other outputs from this project might measure dependence.
codes.note: This is a study of physiological safety (CBC, liver and kidney function) in kratom users compared with non-users. No kratom dependence or use-disorder measure is reported in the text received. The questionnaire (Supplementary File S1) was not provided, but the Methods describe its content and mention no dependence items.

codes.sample: Penang, Malaysia, case-control study. Community snowball recruitment, Jan 2019 to Jan 2020. 60 regular kratom users aged 18–60 (plus 50 controls, not used for prevalence). Excluded: psychiatric or medical illness, illicit drug or alcohol use, positive urine screen, ER-stress medications. 40 of 100 screened users were excluded.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Regular use: daily kratom consumption for 12 consecutive months (lifetime regular or current daily use). Kratom was taken as kratom juice (glasses of about 300 ml).
codes.dependence_measures: A psychiatrist assessed DSM-5 substance use disorder criteria applied to kratom, using all 11 criteria. A case was ≥2 criteria within 12 consecutive months, giving a binary result. The statistics section mentions KDS scores, but no KDS results are reported.

estimates.threshold_or_category: Kratom use disorder (≥2 of 11 criteria in 12 months)
estimates.quote: The prevalence of kratom use disorder among the regular kratom users in this study was 41.7% (n = 25).

codes.possible_duplicate: Penang community sample of 60 regular kratom users, recruited 2019–2020 by the USM/AMDI group (author MFILBA, FRGS/1/2018/SSK02/USM/03/1). Other biomarker papers from this same grant or cohort may use the same users.
codes.note: Users with comorbidity or other drug use were excluded (40 of 100). This is not selection for kratom problems, but it may limit how representative the sample is. No DSM-5 severity categories are reported. KDS is mentioned but no figures are given. Supplementary S2 and S3 tables (characteristics) are not in the text received.

codes.sample: US adults on Amazon mTurk who reported lifetime kratom use in a parent online substance-use survey (Sep 2020–Mar 2021). They were recontacted in April–May 2021, giving N=129 of 289 (44.6%). 51.9% female, 71.9% White, mean age 34.8. 64.3% used kratom in the past year and 45.7% in the past month.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime use (≥1 use of kratom ever); the sample includes current and former users. Past-year use (64.3%) and past-month use (45.7%) are also reported.
codes.dependence_measures: A DSM-5 SUD symptom checklist applied to kratom was given. Only two single criteria are reported here: using to avoid withdrawal (28.7%) and needing larger amounts (33.3%). No KUD case definition or prevalence is reported. KUD is said to be 'the focus of a separate report' (ref 30).
codes.possible_duplicate: Same mTurk kratom recontact sample (US, April–May 2021, N=129) as the separate report on DSM-5 KUD symptoms (ref 30, probably Smith et al. 2022). That companion paper should be screened for KUD prevalence. The parent survey is Smith et al. 2021c (Sep 2020–Mar 2021).
codes.note: Discussion: DSM-5 checklist items 'were selected by 28.7% and 33.3% of the sample... (the focus of a separate report; 30)'. These are single criteria, not a KUD case definition. Tables 1–5 and the supplement are missing from the text, but their descriptions point to demographics, motivations, use and conceptualizations only. The reviewer may want to check them.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a Czech diploma thesis (Charles University, Faculty of Pharmacy, Hradec Králové, 2025) that reviews the literature on kratom botany, pharmacology, traditional use, adverse effects, dependence, prevalence and legal status. It collected no data of its own.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Not applicable, because the thesis has no primary data. Use definitions appear only in its summaries of other people's studies.
codes.dependence_measures: The thesis used no dependence measure of its own. It only describes measures from cited studies, e.g. Singh et al. (2014), which used the Leeds Dependence Questionnaire in 293 regular kratom users in Malaysia (p. 57-58).
codes.possible_duplicate: The only dependence figure (p. 58: more than half severe, "45 % vykazovalo střední závislost" = 45% showed moderate dependence) is second-hand, from Singh et al. 2014 (Drug Alcohol Depend 139:132-137; n=293, Malaysia, LDQ). Extract it from the original paper.
codes.note: This is a narrative literature-review thesis with no primary data, so it is excluded as E5_design. Cited primary sources that may be worth screening: Singh et al. 2014 (LDQ); Koktavá 2024 (Charles University bachelor thesis, 259 Czech kratom users, loss of control; dspace.cuni.cz/handle/20.500.11956/191032); Bačková 2024 (gymnasium students, Zlín region).

Also a 0-100 VAS for how troubled people felt by their use, and SOWS for withdrawal; neither has a case cut-off.

codes.sample: 395 US adults who use kratom regularly, enrolled nationwide July–November 2022 into a remote NIH ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study with a baseline survey. 54.9% male, mean age 38.1, 81.3% White, mean 5.7 years of kratom use. Most used whole-leaf products (95.9%). Not recruited because of kratom problems.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Current regular use ("US adults who use kratom regularly"; "active US adult kratom consumers"). KUD reported for lifetime and past year.
codes.dependence_measures: DSM-5 SUD criteria applied to kratom: all 11 criteria (KUD), self-report survey. Any KUD = 2+ symptoms; mild = 2–3; moderate = 4–5; severe = 6+. Given for both lifetime and past-year symptoms. SOWS (withdrawal only) was also used, but it is not a dependence measure.

Past-year KUD (2+ past-year symptoms) was met by 46.6%

codes.possible_duplicate: Same sample as other reports from the NIH (Smith et al.) nationwide US kratom EMA study, July–Nov 2022, n=395 surveyed: Smith et al. 2023a (methods), Smith et al. 2023b (in-depth interviews), and Smith et al. 2024 (EMA and observed dosing). Check those for overlapping KUD estimates.
codes.note: Percentages only. The n of 395 is assumed (survey completers); no n is given for the KUD items. Supplementary Table 1 (KUD counts and severity) was not received; check it for counts. Abstract's "mostly in the mild/moderate range (80.7%)" is ambiguous and was not extracted. No sex-specific prevalences.

codes.sample: NSDUH 2021–2024, a nationally representative cross-sectional US household survey of non-institutionalised people aged 12 and older. The abstract gives n=169,408 analysed; the Methods give a sample size of 232,441. The text does not give the number of kratom users in each subgroup.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime, prior-to-past-year and past-year kratom use, asked as "if they had used kratom in any form including powder, pills, or leaf".
codes.dependence_measures: NSDUH proxy past-year DSM-5 SUD from drug-specific questions on cannabis, prescription opioids, sedatives/tranquilizers, stimulants and other drugs. Kratom use disorder is not assessed; the figure reported is any past-year SUD among kratom users.
codes.possible_duplicate: Uses the public NSDUH data (2021–2024, US). Other secondary analyses of NSDUH kratom data from overlapping years may draw on the same respondents.
codes.note: 52.8% (95% CI 50.1–55.4) of prior-to-past-year kratom users had a past-year DSM-5 SUD. This is SUD for any substance, not kratom use disorder; the SUD items cover other drugs and kratom is not listed, so I3/I4 are not met for kratom. Table 2 and the supplement are missing, but nothing suggests kratom-specific SUD was measured.

codes.sample: Anonymous US online convenience survey, Dec 2023–Jul 2024. Adults ≥18 were eligible if they reported lifetime use of kratom, kava, tianeptine and/or akuamma seed. N=368 in total; 180 reported lifetime kava use. Of these 180, 82.2% also reported lifetime kratom use. The paper reports no total count of kratom users across the full sample.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime kratom use. It was an inclusion option for the survey, and for kava users it appears only as a figure in Supplemental Table 1 ("kratom (82.2%)"). No kratom-specific analysis.
codes.dependence_measures: No kratom use-disorder or dependence measure is reported here. The text says SUD findings are "presented elsewhere [24]". It reports a self-reported history of any SUD diagnosis, but not kratom-specific, and kava perceptions ("habit-forming", "addictive").
codes.possible_duplicate: Same survey (US online, Dec 2023–Jul 2024, N=368) as Hill, Boyer, Smith, "Clinically characterizing adults who use kava or kratom..." Drug Alcohol Depend Rep 2025;17:100394 (ref 24). That paper reports the SUD results; screen it for kratom estimates.
codes.note: This paper is about kava. Kratom appears only as an inclusion criterion and as a co-use percentage. The only SUD items are general: self-reported history of any SUD diagnosis (not by substance) and kava conceptualizations. P.2: "Other findings from this project related to substance use disorder for kava are presented elsewhere [24]"; p.9 says the same. Check ref 24.

codes.sample: US adults who use kratom regularly (at least 3 times/week for at least 4 weeks before screening), recruited online and through kratom stakeholders, July–November 2022; baseline survey N=395; 357 completed the 15-day EMA. Recruited for kratom use, not for kratom problems.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Current regular use: "at least three times a week for a minimum of four weeks prior to screening".
codes.dependence_measures: No kratom use-disorder or dependence results in this report. DSM-5 past-year SUD criteria for kratom were reported in the parent study ("past-year criteria for substance use disorder for kratom... have been previously reported.18"). Only BPI pain measures used here.
codes.possible_duplicate: Secondary analysis of the NIH US EMA study of regular kratom consumers (ref 18, primary outcomes; ref 19, methods). Same N=395 baseline / N=357 EMA sample, recruited July–Nov 2022. Ref 18 reports past-year DSM-5 SUD criteria for kratom; check it for eligibility.
codes.note: The only related item is BPI-adapted: "concerned that you take too much kratom for pain" (7.1% yes, 83.7% no, among those with chronic pain). This is not a dependence measure with a cut-off. The 12.3%–29.5% kratom use disorder in the Discussion comes from other studies. Retrieve ref 18 for this cohort's DSM-5 estimates.

codes.sample: Cross-sectional rs-fMRI study with a convenience sample. 10 male regular kratom users (mean age 27.30 ± 3.97) and 7 healthy male controls from the same community in Malaysia, scanned at the Imaging Unit, USM Bertam Medical Centre, Penang.
codes.kratom_use_definition: "self-reported regular kratom users consuming at least three glasses (300 mL each) of kratom solution daily for a minimum of one year" (p.3). This is current daily use of kratom decoction lasting at least 1 year.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only data collected were kratom use history (age at first use, duration, quantity, frequency), CANTAB cognitive tests and fMRI. The KDS and COWS appear only in the limitations section, as recommendations for future studies (p.8).
codes.possible_duplicate: May overlap with other USM Centre for Drug Research neuroimaging and cognition papers on regular male kratom users scanned at USM Bertam, for example Singh, Chye et al. 2018 (brain MRI, MJMHS) and Singh et al. 2018b (cognition). Mitragynine content is taken from 'the same sample' (p.3).
codes.note: The study population is regular kratom users who were not recruited because of kratom problems, but no use-disorder or dependence instrument was given. The paper describes the KDS as something future studies should add: "Screening tools, such as relevant questionnaires like the Kratom Dependence Scale (KDS)... should also be incorporated" (p.8). There is no dependence prevalence to extract.

codes.sample: US adults recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk, Sept 2020–March 2021 (2615 evaluable surveys). The analysed subsample is people who reported past-year kratom use, N = 174 (115 of them also reported past-month use). They came from the "opioid-stimulant group", defined by past-6-month use of an opioid, a stimulant or kratom. They were not recruited because of kratom problems.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Past-year kratom use (N = 174). Past-month use is also reported (n = 115).
codes.dependence_measures: DSM-5 SUD checklist (mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe ≥6) for each person's "biggest problem" or most-used substance. Kratom was rated for only n = 27 (14 biggest problem, 13 most used); no kratom-specific results reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same NIDA IRP MTurk survey (Sept 2020–Mar 2021, 2615 evaluable surveys; 174 past-year kratom users). The text says kratom-specific DSM SUD responses "were assessed in detail elsewhere" (ref 74). That companion paper probably reports kratom use disorder figures for this sample and should be checked.
codes.note: Table 1 SUD severity (None 17%, Mild 16%, Moderate 21%, Severe 47%; 82.8% any SUD) is for any substance, mostly not kratom. The text says: "Analyses here will not focus on kratom-specific DSM SUD responses, as these were assessed in detail elsewhere." So there is no kratom use disorder estimate here; look up ref 74.

codes.sample: 10 US adults who use kratom regularly (6 men, 4 women, mean age 41.2), re-recruited July–November 2022 from a 15-day remote study (NCT05457803). Each lived within 150 miles of the NIH clinic and self-administered their typical morning kratom dose under direct observation.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Regular use: "report using kratom ≥3 times weekly for ≥4 weeks before enrollment". Seven used kratom 7 days/week, 2 used it 5 days/week and 1 used it 3 days/week.
codes.dependence_measures: No use-disorder or dependence measure. The only related measure was the Subjective Opioid Withdrawal Scale (SOWS), a withdrawal scale. The other outcomes were ARCI, DEQ, vital signs and psychomotor tasks.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is a substudy of the NIH natural-history study NCT05457803 (15-day remote study, US, 2022). Interview and driving-simulation results from the same 10 participants are reported elsewhere (ref 12).
codes.note: Lab study, n=10. The only symptom scale was SOWS, a withdrawal scale; all baseline scores were in the mild range (1-10). No DSM-5, ICD, SDS or other dependence instrument was applied to kratom. Physical dependence is mentioned only from interviews, with no count. The parent remote study (NCT05457803) may report kratom use disorder data; screen it separately.

codes.sample: Two US samples. (1) mTurk online convenience sample, Sep 2020–Mar 2021, adults reporting past-6-month alcohol, opioid and/or illicit stimulant use, N=2,615; 289 lifetime and 174 past-year kratom users. (2) NSDUH 2019 adults aged 18+ (weighted proportions only; no kratom-user n reported).
codes.kratom_use_definition: Self-reported lifetime kratom use (n=289) and past-year kratom use (n=174) in the mTurk sample; lifetime and past-year use in NSDUH 2019.
codes.dependence_measures: mTurk: DSM-5 SUD checklist completed for ONE substance, either the one with the "biggest problem" or the most-used one, not specifically kratom; moderate-severe = more than 3 criteria. NSDUH: UDPYILL (past-year DSM-IV dependence/abuse of illicit drugs). Neither gives a kratom-specific diagnosis.
codes.possible_duplicate: The mTurk sample (Sep 2020–Mar 2021, N=2,615) is the same one used in Smith et al. 2021c/d (kratom dose-effect paper). Those papers may report kratom-specific DSM-5 data; check them. NSDUH 2019 kratom data were also analysed by Palamar 2021.
codes.note: Table 1 (p.5): "Moderate - Severe SUD" for 193/289 lifetime (66.78%) and 117/174 past-year (67.24%) kratom users. This is SUD for the respondent's "biggest problem" or most-used substance, not kratom (p.4), so it is not kratom use disorder. For NSDUH, only kratom-use proportions by illicit-drug dependence/abuse status are given.

codes.sample: 22 regular adult kratom users and 20 non-kratom users (controls) who had fMRI scans for an earlier USM study (USM/JEPEM/19010053). Cross-sectional fMRI analysis, Malaysia (IPPT/AMDI Bertam, Penang; HUSM). Master of Medicine (Radiology) dissertation, Universiti Sains Malaysia, 2023.
codes.kratom_use_definition: "regular kratom adult kratom users" (Abstract), also described as "long-term consumption". The retrieved text gives no exact frequency or duration criterion; the inclusion criteria (section 3.5.1) are not in the text.
codes.dependence_measures: None found in the retrieved text. The available parts (abstracts, Ch. 1–2) mention no DSM, ICD, KDS, SDS, ASSIST or diagnostic interview. Ch. 3 (methods, research tool) and Ch. 4 (results manuscript) are missing.
codes.possible_duplicate: The fMRI data come from an earlier USM study (USM/JEPEM/19010053) of kratom users and non-users scanned at rest and during inspiration, so the sample may overlap with other USM kratom neuroimaging papers (Penang).
codes.note: Text truncated at Ch. 2: methods (3.5–3.6), results (Ch. 4) and appendices are missing. Neuroimaging study (brainstem BOLD) with no dependence measure in the available text, so likely E4_no_dependence_measure. Check the full PDF methods/appendices for any screening tool before excluding. Users are called "kratom addicts" once (sec. 2.3), but no instrument is given.

codes.sample: This is a school survey of 8th and 9th graders from 4 randomly selected primary schools in the Nymburk district, Czech Republic, done with a paper questionnaire in November 2023. There were 287 respondents aged 13–15 (163 boys, 121 girls, 3 other). 51 of them (17.8%) reported lifetime kratom use (32 boys, 19 girls).
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime any use. Q8 asked "Vyzkoušel jsi někdy v životě kratom?" ("Have you ever tried kratom in your life?"), answered Ano/Ne (yes/no). 51 of 287 answered yes.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The 12-item questionnaire covered lifetime use, number of times used, how kratom was obtained, reasons for use, knowledge of effects and risks, and attitudes. It used no DSM, ICD, dependence scale or ASSIST.
codes.possible_duplicate: Bachelor's thesis (Charles University, 1st Faculty of Medicine, 2023). Sample: 287 pupils in the Nymburk district, November 2023. No overlapping publication is known.
codes.note: The thesis is in Czech. It reports only lifetime use prevalence, frequency categories (once 41.2%, twice 19.6%, about five times 27.4%, ten or more times 11.8% of the 51 users), sources, motives, knowledge and attitudes. "Závislost" (dependence) appears only as a risk that pupils picked in a knowledge question. It is not an assessment of the pupils themselves.

codes.sample: Secondary analysis of NHMS 2019, Malaysia: a nationally representative household survey of 10,472 adults aged 18 and over (two-stage stratified random sampling). Past-30-day kratom use had a weighted prevalence of 0.40% (95% CI 0.22–0.56). The report gives no unweighted count of kratom users.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Past 30 days: "During the past 30 days, did you use these types of drug/substances? ... 4) kratom" (self-administered questionnaire).
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study measured only current use of tobacco, alcohol and drugs (including kratom) and grouped people with latent class analysis. It used no DSM, ICD, ASSIST or dependence scale for kratom.
codes.possible_duplicate: Uses NHMS 2019 data (Malaysia, n=10,472 adults). Other NHMS 2019 publications on substance use may use the same sample.
codes.note: The report gives only the prevalence of kratom use (Table 2) and polysubstance-use classes from latent class analysis. It does not assess kratom use disorder or dependence. The data availability section mentions 'NHMS 2017', which looks like a typo for the 2019 survey.

codes.sample: A convenience sample of 1,098 people applying for methadone maintenance treatment at 11 clinics in 7 US states (AL, MI, NJ, NC, OH, OK, PA), Sept 2020–Nov 2022; 43.2% female; mean age 37.4. The text gives no size for the kratom-positive subsample.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Recent use found by testing: a positive LC-MS-MS result for mitragynine (kratom) in oral fluid or urine. The text gives no count of positive tests.
codes.dependence_measures: None. Substance use was measured only by toxicology. The study used no SUD, dependence scale or diagnostic interview for kratom or any other substance.
codes.possible_duplicate: The same toxicology project (methadone intake clinics, 2020–2022) may be reported in Lee-Easton et al., 2024 and Magura et al., 2023, which the authors cite.
codes.note: Methods: "two substances (trazodone and mitragynine) with particular clinical significance"; "mitragynine (kratom)". The study gives only polysubstance prevalence from testing. Full tables of substance combinations are in supplementary material that was not received, but nothing suggests it contains any dependence measure. The exclusion applies whatever is in the supplement.

codes.sample: Thai national household survey, Jul–Dec 2016. Stratified five-stage cluster sample of people aged 15–64, N=30,411 (93.8% response). Kratom leaf use was 15.1% lifetime, 2.1% past year and 1.4% past month. Kratom cocktail use was 14.5% lifetime, 0.7% past year and 0.4% past month. The text gives no absolute n of kratom users.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime use (at least once ever), past-year use (at least once in the past 12 months) and past-month use (at least once in the past 30 days), reported separately for kratom leaves and kratom cocktail. 'Habitual use' (>20 days in the past month) is reported only for all NPS combined.
codes.dependence_measures: The questionnaire included the WHO ASSIST (Tools section), but no ASSIST scores or risk bands are reported for kratom or any other substance. 'Habitual use' (>5 days/week or >20 days/month) is a use-frequency measure, not a dependence measure.
codes.possible_duplicate: 2016 Thailand national household survey on substance use (Khon Kaen University ethics approval HE581329; N=30,411; July–December 2016). Other publications or ACSAN reports from this survey might report ASSIST results for kratom users.
codes.note: The WHO ASSIST was given, which counts as a dependence/risk measure under I3, but the paper reports only use prevalence (Table 2) and habitual NPS use for all NPS combined (Table 4). No ASSIST risk-band counts are given for kratom users, so this paper has no extractable dependence estimate. It may be worth looking for other reports from the same survey dataset that give ASSIST results for kratom.

codes.sample: 400 Thai male conscripts at a fort in Ratchaburi Province who had been in the fort more than 3 months, interviewed July–September 2023. Subsamples: lifetime users of kratom leaves (n=208, 52.0%) and lifetime users of kratom leaf decoction mixtures (n=143, 35.8%). Past-3-month use was 133 and 88 respectively.
codes.kratom_use_definition: Lifetime any use, with kratom leaves and 'mixtures of kratom leaf decoction' (4x100) reported separately. Tables 4 and 5 use the lifetime-user n's (208 and 143) as denominators, not the past-3-month users.
codes.dependence_measures: (1) Substance Use Disorder Screening Test (SUDST, Saengduenchai et al. 2023), based on DSM-5: 11 yes/no items, past 12 months. Scores 2–3 = low (mild), 4–5 = moderate, ≥6 = high (severe). (2) WHO ASSIST v3.1, Thai version, risk bands: low 0–3, moderate 4–26, high ≥27.
